title: Modelos de nube
description: Service models, deployment models, and the shared responsibility split.
rows: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service)
Physical data center, hardware, hypervisor, storage, and network fabric.
Guest OS and its patching, middleware, applications, data, identities, and network security settings (security groups).
Virtual machines in a public cloud. Most customer responsibility of the three main models.
PaaS (Platform as a Service)
Everything in IaaS plus the OS, runtime, and middleware.
Application code, its configuration, data, and access.
Managed app hosting or managed databases. Customer still owns secure coding and data.
SaaS (Software as a Service)
The entire application stack, including the application itself.
Data, user accounts and access, and the app's security settings.
Hosted email or CRM. Least customer responsibility, but data and access are always the customer's.
FaaS / serverless
Servers, OS, runtime, and scaling.
Function code, its permissions, and data.
Code runs only when triggered. No servers to patch, but over-permissive function roles are a common risk.
XaaS (Anything as a Service)
Varies with the specific service.
Varies; always data and access.
Umbrella term for any capability delivered as a cloud service.
MaaS (Monitoring as a Service)
Monitoring platform, collection infrastructure, and often analysts.
Deciding what to monitor, providing access to sources, and acting on alerts.
Outsourced monitoring of systems or security events.
Public cloud
Multi-tenant infrastructure owned and run by the CSP.
Their own workloads, configuration, and data.
Shared with other tenants; lowest upfront cost, least physical control.
Private cloud
The organization itself, or a vendor dedicated to that one organization.
Effectively everything when self-hosted; if a vendor hosts it, the split follows the contract.
Single tenant; more control and compliance flexibility at higher cost.
Community cloud
Shared among organizations with common requirements, run by one of them or a third party.
Their own workloads; governance is shared among members.
Example: agencies or hospitals sharing a compliant environment.
Hybrid cloud
Each environment's provider or owner manages its part.
Integration, consistent security policy, and identity across environments.
Mix of public and private/on-premises. Complexity and consistent policy are the classic exam concerns.
Multi-cloud
Each CSP manages its own platform.
Policy, identity, and visibility across several providers.
Avoids vendor lock-in and a single provider outage (a resilience strategy in 3.4).
Shared responsibility (always)
Physical security of data centers and the underlying infrastructure in every model.
Data, classification, and identity/access management in every model.
CompTIA calls the written split a responsibility matrix. If a question asks who protects the data, the answer is the customer.
